passage:
Pranav's first Monday as team lead began with a joke. "Congratulations, boss," said Dolma, with a flat smile. She had wanted the role, and her comments in meetings came out sharp. Pranav's cheeks warmed, and he wondered if they all thought he did not deserve it. He told the team, "I don't know the billing system as well as Dolma does, so I will lean on her." He listened more than he talked, and gave Dolma the client migration, big work with her name on it. He did not demand warmth.

Mridul followed the new plan and thanked him after the review. "That was clear." Pranav felt proud, and also unsure. Each week he asked, "What is one thing I could do better?" and passed credit for the win to the team.

By the second month he was lost on budgeting and hesitated to ask his director. Then he wrote three lines: "Here is my problem, here are two options, which would you choose?" The director spent half an hour with him and suggested a coach. "You should have asked sooner," the director said, smiling.

By spring Dolma had started bringing him ideas. It took time, and neither of them mentioned it.

qa.q: What work did Pranav give Dolma?
qa.a: He gave Dolma the client migration.

qa.q: How did Pranav's approach to Dolma's coolness compare with his handling of Mridul's thanks?
qa.a: With Dolma he stayed generous and gave her meaningful work without demanding warmth. With Mridul's thanks he felt proud yet unsure, so he kept asking for feedback and passed credit to the team.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling when Dolma said "Congratulations, boss" with a flat smile?
qa.a: He felt hurt and unsure, wondering if the team thought he did not deserve the role.

qa.q: What made Pranav's request to his director work well?
qa.a: He brought a specific problem with two options instead of just worry, and the director gave him half an hour and a coach.

grounding: A new manager over former peers feels doubt, meets thanks and a passed-over colleague's coolness, and learns to ask his own director for coaching early.
